newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Wall Street awaits Fed, on edge.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Wall Street awaits Fed, on edge.

text.p: The big question for Wall Street next week is whether U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan will act to raise interest rates, and many analysts forecast a weak and volatile market no matter the answer.

The Federal Reserve Open Market Committee, which guides U.S. interest rates, is set to meet on Tuesday and Fed-watchers are divided as to whether it will strike against inflation by boosting rates by 25 basis points or more.

"It all depends on the Fed, but I see the high volatility continuing indefinitely," said Edgar Peters, chief investment strategist and director of asset allocation at Boston-based PanAgora Asset Management.
On Friday the Dow ended off 139 points at 7194, after closing at a record high 7333.55 on Thursday. For the week, the blue chip gauge rose 25.
If the Fed raises interest rates, analysts said the stock market will fall because optimistic investors have not priced in a hike and market valuation is rich.

"I think it's time for a (market) correction," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "The market is trading at the high end of its range, we will likely see a rate hike and we are having problems with the dollar and money flows into dollar instruments."

Sam Stovall, an analyst at S&P Industry Reports, said his strategy group believed there was a "better-than-even" chance the Federal Reserve would raise rates, although the group was less convinced than it was last week.

"I don't think investors have factored in another rate hike so it could throw cold water and force them to rethink things for a week or so," Stovall said. But he said investors were still buying on dips and any sell-off would be short.
Even if the Federal Reserve decided inflation was mild enough to leave interest rates alone, the stock market was still poised to give up ground, analysts said.

"At some time, there is probably going to be a pause," A.C. Moore, a market analyst at Principal Financial Securities said. "We could see selling on the news (that the Fed opted not to raise rates), with nothing left for markets to digest."

PanAgora's Ed Peters, who said he thought the Federal Reserve might be behind the inflation-fighting curve and forecast a rate boost, said: "If the Fed doesn't raise rates, I think we are in for choppy volatility. From here on in, while the Fed is in tightening mode, the market is susceptible to shocks from bad news."
With shares trading near record levels, analysts said the stock market was vulnerable to bad news and could face competition from bonds offering attractive yields.
"I think the Fed will raise rates, I don't think the bond market will take it well and I expect to see tactical asset allocators shift money into bonds," Metz said.
Some analysts said investors viewed last week's reports on April wholesale and retail inflation data as relatively benign and underestimated the threat higher prices posed to the economy.

"Everyone seems to be forgetting that inflation does not move up until unemployment bottoms out and the Fed moves to try and preempt inflation," Peters said. "And if the Fed does not raise rates, it will be because they think the economy is slowing on its own, and that does not bode well for earnings."
Other events next week like the release of international trade data by the U.S. Commerce Department on Wednesday, would pale in comparison to the Fed meeting, analysts said.
"Whatever happens next week will happen early in the week and the rest of the week will be spent trying to sort things out if there is anything to sort out," Stovall said.
